The left branch is a 12 V power supply, and the figure indicates that its upper terminal is negative and its lower terminal is positive; the upper-left node is connected through a diode D to the upper output node. The middle branch, from the upper output node downward in sequence, consists of a 3 kΩ resistor and a 9 V power supply; in the figure, the upper terminal of the 9 V power supply is negative and the lower terminal is positive, and the bottom terminal is connected to the lower common wire. Reasoning: Take the lower common wire as 0 V. Since the lower terminal of the 9 V power supply is positive and connected to 0 V, and the upper terminal is negative, the potential of the upper-terminal node of the 9 V power supply is -9 V. The output terminal is open-circuited, and first treating the diode as non-conducting, then there is no current in the 3 kΩ resistor and no voltage drop across the resistor, so the upper output node is also -9 V. Then use the left-side 12 V power supply to check consistency: the lower terminal of the 12 V power supply is connected to 0 V and is positive, and the upper terminal is negative, so the upper-left node is -12 V. The left side of the diode is -12 V and the right-side output node is -9 V, so the diode is reverse-biased, and the non-conducting assumption holds. The marked polarity of U0 is that the lower terminal is positive and the upper terminal is negative, so U0 = Vlower - Vupper = 0 - (-9) = 9 V.
